title: SciCode: A Research Coding Benchmark Curated by Scientists

model.params_source: assumed (paper silent; the released inspect_ai command runs with temperature 0)

task.subset_rule: all 338 subproblems of the 80 test problems (standard setup: no background, generated solutions to previous subproblems carried over)
task.approximation: none beyond the local Python execution environment

items.source: SciCode1/SciCode, file problems_test.jsonl (80 problems); numeric test targets test_data.h5 from the Google Drive folder linked in https://github.com/scicode-bench/SciCode

prompt.user_template:
PROBLEM DESCRIPTION:
You will be provided with problem steps along with background knowledge necessary for solving the problem. Your task will be to develop a Python solution focused on the next step of the problem-solving process.
PROBLEM STEPS AND FUNCTION CODE:
Here, you'll find the Python code for the initial steps of the problem-solving process. This code is integral to building the solution.
{problem_steps_str}
NEXT STEP - PROBLEM STEP AND FUNCTION HEADER:
This part will describe the next step in the problem-solving process. A function header will be provided, and your task is to develop the Python code for this next step based on the provided description and function header.
{next_step_str}
DEPENDENCIES:
Use only the following dependencies in your solution. Do not include these dependencies at the beginning of your code.
{dependencies}
RESPONSE GUIDELINES:
1. Start with the scientific background required for the next step, formatted as a comment.
2. Then write the complete and executable Python program for the next step in a single block.
3. Your response should focus exclusively on implementing the solution for the next step, adhering closely to the specified function header and the context provided by the initial steps.
4. DO NOT include previous function code, example usage or test code in your response.
5. Ensure your response is in the format of ```python``` and includes the necessary background as a comment at the top.
Example:
```python
# Background: [Here, insert the necessary scientific knowledge required for the next step.]
[Insert the Python code here based on the provided function header and dependencies.]
```

placeholders.problem_steps_str: previous sub-steps + the model's own earlier generations (sequential dependency; not expressible)
placeholders.next_step_str: sub_steps[k].step_description_prompt + sub_steps[k].function_header (per sub-step; list indexing not expressible)

prompt.verbatim: full (the extraction rendered ```python``` as curly quotes and dropped the code fence and '# ' marker of the Example block; restored following the released template)

placeholders_paper.problem_steps_str: previous subproblem descriptions each followed by the model's own generated code for that step (standard setup); empty for the first step
placeholders_paper.next_step_str: step_description_prompt + function_header of the current subproblem

output.postprocess: prepend dependencies; execute with the subproblem's test_cases and test_data.h5 targets; no fenced block = fail

metric.name: custom
metric.definition: subproblem pass@1 = share of the 338 subproblems whose single generated function passes all of its test cases.

cost.prepare_note: runner --prepare failed: placeholder spec not machine-readable: "previous sub-steps + the model's own earlier generations (sequential dependency; not expressible)"

open_points: Protocol beyond one main stage: each sub-step prompt embeds the model's own code for the previous sub-steps (sequential, stateful calls per problem), which the runner's single-stage battery cannot express.
pass@1 needs the generated functions executed against sub_steps[].test_cases with the test_data.h5 targets (Google Drive) in a scientific-Python sandbox; no code execution in the runner or hooks.
problems_test.jsonl holds 65 problems / 291 sub-steps; the paper's 80 / 338 add the 15 dev problems (problems_dev.jsonl) - confirm which set the Table 2 column uses.
